A marmot stands bolt upright on a boulder at the edge of the old snow patch, forepaws tucked, small against the white expanse behind it.
A pika trots across loose flat stones with a mouthful of yellow and purple flower stems jutting out sideways, a whole sideways bouquet wider than its head.
Two marmots lie flat out and sprawling on the same sun-warmed granite slab, side by side, small against the slab's grey width.
An ibex moves across a loose scree slope above the last flowers, each hoof placed with care, tiny against the grey-brown rock face rising behind it.
A line of bighorn sheep picks along a narrow ledge high on the rock face, their pale bodies strung out in single file, small against the vertical stone.
A ptarmigan stands absolutely still among the low yellow flowers, half its body still white from winter, the rest already mottled brown, invisible until it is not.
Twenty or more small orange butterflies work a single clump of deep-violet flowers growing flat against the ground, old grey snow lying a few inches away.
A dozen or more bumblebees hang low and heavy over a sweep of white flowers hugging the ground out of the wind, moving slowly in the cold thin air.
An alpine crow, glossy black with a bright yellow beak, stands on a bare granite slab at the meadow's edge, the long slope of old snow stretching behind it.
An ermine in its brown summer coat sits up between two large rocks, its white chest catching the light, small against the boulders that dwarf it on both sides.
A mountain goat stands on a slab no wider than its own body, small and white against the grey-blue snowfield that fills the upper frame above it.
A marmot runs full tilt through the flowers, its tail straight out behind it like a rudder, small against the scree slope it is racing toward.
A golden eagle hangs motionless and tiny against the bright white of the snowfield, its shadow sliding dark across the meadow far below it.
A mountain hare presses flat against bare ground in the lee of a large rock, its coat half-brown half-white, almost the same colour as the patchy snow beside the rock.
A snow vole pauses on a flat grey stone between two clumps of tiny pink flowers growing tight and low against the ground, its body barely longer than the flowers are wide.
A chamois stands at the very top of a long scree run, looking down, small and dark against the pale broken stone that fills the whole slope below it.
A ptarmigan and its own reflection sit in a shallow meltwater pool between two rocks, the bird's half-white feathers and their mirror image both vivid against the dark water.
A dozen or more bumblebees crowd a clump of bright red flowers growing in short stiff spikes no higher than the rock beside them, the bees blurring with motion.
A pika sits completely still on a pale stone beside a large patch of cut flower stems it has laid out to dry in the sun, its round ears huge on its small face.
A marmot stands on a rock at the top of the old snow patch's uphill edge, its shadow falling long and sharp across the white surface below it.
Twenty or more small blue butterflies lift all at once from a low dense spread of white flowers, a sudden blue cloud against the dark rock face behind them.
A mountain goat descends a near-vertical rock face above the flower line, its four legs splayed at impossible angles, tiny against the enormous slab it grips.
An ibex stands with its forelegs up on a large boulder at the meadow's edge, its long ridged horns curving back against the sky, small against the boulder's mass.
A golden eagle drops fast and steep toward the far end of the meadow, its wings half-folded, tiny against the white wall of the snowfield it has fallen away from.

A dozen or more bumblebees and twenty or more small yellow butterflies work the same long sweep of purple and orange flowers growing dense and low across the broken ground, the two crowds moving through each other without touching.
